content:
I would like to make some contributions to CSLib. I notice that under the lambda calculus theme, there has been active development for locally nameless representation, but the named representation has been silent for a while. So I think it's a good idea to contribute to the named representation. I wanted to check that this direction is still in the roadmap, and that there is not someone else working on it currently to avoid duplicate work.

I understand that formalising named representation has been notoriously difficult. The Barendregt convention is difficult to deal with, and there is easily a mutual dependence between the definition of alpha conversion and capture-avoiding substitution. See this explanation from Nominal Isabelle.

For example, there is currently a theorem listed as TODO in the repository:

theorem Term.subst_comm
  [DecidableEq Var] [HasFresh Var]
  {m : Term Var} {x : Var} {n1 : Term Var} {y : Var} {n2 : Term Var} :
  (m[x := n1])[y := n2] = (m[y := n2])[x := n1]

This theorem is not correct in its current form, and the correct form can be found in the above link. But even the correct form won't work here, because there is no guarantee about the fresh variables introduced during the capture-avoiding substitution, and the best we can say is that the two terms are alpha-equivalent, a notion that has not been introduced yet.

I am thinking of following the definition from Nominal Techniques, formula (7) (but the nominal techniques themselves do not have to be involved). As first step, we define a (non-capture-avoiding) naive variable renaming that works on both free and bound variables. As second step, we define a notion of alpha-equivalence that is equivalent to Barendregt 1984, but (in my opinion) is neater as it is based on structural induction on the term, and rules such as refl, symm, and trans can be introduced as theorems, not definitions. As third step, we define capture-avoiding substitution.

In most, if not all, future developments based on this, equality (sameness) between terms shall be referred to as alpha-equivalence. This may complicate things a bit, but I guess this is what you have to live with with named representation.

I am planning to starting experimenting with this approach. Does this design align with the roadmap of CSLib?

I am focusing on well scoped de Bruijn indicies as a test of some metaprogramming utilities and others are continuing to develop under the locally nameless binding. AFAIK there are no immediate plans to work on this named representation, so I don't think there is a problem with duplicating work.

I believe this named module predates me being a maintainer and I am not too surprised if the definitions have some issues as they've not been used. I would be happy to review work fleshing this out. There has been some other discussion about nominal sets in general (cc @Bas Spitters), and I would be welcoming of whatever background you need if you're wanting to closely follow Nominal Isabelle.

I wrote the named Lambda Calculus module as an exploration of how (the beginning of) the 'usual' pen-and-paper version would look like. I'd welcome further development of it, but as Chris mentions, I'm not working on it right now (nor I'm aware of others doing so), so no risk of overlap.

My bad for not removing that theorem, I sketched it to test substitutions and left it there after realising it was wrong later on, sorry.

My mid-term thoughts for this were that:

  • It'd be nice to prove one day a theorem connecting the other representations of lambda calculus to the named representation, to show what is formally meant by their 'adequacy'.
  • We do need to investigate alpha-equivalence (which is the complicated part, as you point out).

Re alpha-equivalence, I'd be very interested in your definition. From what you say, we could prove that it is the same as the current one. I'd like that as well. :-)

Yes, proofs of equivalence would be nice. I had thought maybe the proposed FaithfullyEncoded and FullyEncoded (from this thread) is a relevant way to state some of this?

I will also note again that there is recent work on joint semantics of these different bindings: Categorical Foundations of First-Order Abstract Syntax. This is formalized in Rocq already, so there is something to closely reference if anyone is interested in this sort of work.

Thank you for the explanations. I have now completed the first two steps I sketched above, i.e., a definition of alpha equivalence and some of its basic properties. My plan is to open a PR once I finish the proofs for basic properties of capture-avoiding substitution, including the "commutativity" lemma we discussed above as a touchstone. But you can check here if you want to have an idea of what how I'm doing now.

I agree that equivalence between different representations is an interesting thing to work on.

For alpha-equivalence, the proof that the definition I'm using (by Gabbay and Pitts) coincides with Barendregt's famous definition (i.e. the definition by Fabrizio in the current repository) can be found in their original paper. And I'm happy to work on this equivalence as a next step.

For different representations of lambda calculus, the FullyEncoded approach seems feasible to me, and I'm happy to assist once the definition of named representation is stablised. If this works, then it seems that the workload for named lambda calculus can be greatly reduced, as the proof for semantic properties such as Church-Rosser or normalisation of STLC can just use the results from e.g. the locally nameless representation.

PS. A paper Alpha equivalence equalities discuss the equivalence between "five" different definitions of alpha equivalence. But I find some of these definitions are just too similar, and there are just essentially two kinds of definition: the Gabbay & Pitts one and the Barendrget one.

PS 2. I seem to find that grind sometimes cannot recognise a hypothesis that is essentially the same but written using a different notation. A minimal example would be

/-- α-equivalence. -/
inductive Term.AlphaEquiv [DecidableEq Var] : Term Var → Term Var → Prop where
| var {x} : AlphaEquiv (var x) (var x)
| abs {y x1 x2 m1 m2} : y ∉ m1.vars ∪ m2.vars ∪ {x1, x2} →
  AlphaEquiv (m1.rename x1 y) (m2.rename x2 y) → AlphaEquiv (abs x1 m1) (abs x2 m2)
| app {m1 n1 m2 n2} : AlphaEquiv m1 n1 → AlphaEquiv m2 n2 → AlphaEquiv (app m1 m2) (app n1 n2)

/-- Instance for the notation `m =α n`. -/
instance instHasAlphaEquivTerm [DecidableEq Var] : HasAlphaEquiv (Term Var) where
  AlphaEquiv := Term.AlphaEquiv

lemma AlphaEquiv_identity [DecidableEq Var] {m n : Term Var} :
  AlphaEquiv m n → m =α n := by
  intro h
  -- failed:
  -- grind
  -- succeeded:
  assumption

Here grind fails because it does not realise AlphaEquiv and =α are the same thing. Is this intended and is there a way to get around this?
You can have a rfl theorem for the notation that grind uses, see for instance LocallyNameless.Fsub.Ty.subst_def (and then everywhere else from that point on use the notation).
The PR is now available at #458
Thank you very much, that looks pretty good at a first glance. It might be good to add some grind annotations, especially for alpha-equivalence, I guess? What do you think as well, @Chris Henson?
(would probably help with shortening some of the proofs, too)
Yes, it looks reasonable at first glance. I'll make some grind suggestions while reviewing. I am traveling next week and the PR is a bit large, so it may take me a bit.
I believe I have fixed all CI errors now. Feel free to run CI again to check whether it works.
Hi. Are there any updates on this PR?
I'm sorry, I've been pretty behind on reviews. I'm taking some time today and may be able to get started on it.

Haoxuan Yin said:

PS. A paper Alpha equivalence equalities discuss the equivalence between "five" different definitions of alpha equivalence. But I find some of these definitions are just too similar, and there are just essentially two kinds of definition: the Gabbay & Pitts one and the Barendrget one.

Do you know whether the Isabelle/HOL formalization mentioned in Section 7 was ever completed? The paper mentions it as future work by Luana Fagarasa, but I couldn't find anything public.

I'm still fairly new to lambda calculus and binding representations, but I've been trying to read around alpha-equivalence and nominal techniques to understand the different approaches a bit better. Since there seems to be ongoing interest in the named (nominal) representation, I was also wondering whether there are papers (worth a formalization) or existing formalizations you'd particularly recommend reading alongside this development.

I am not an expert in this area so am unable to answer many of your questions. But I want to clarify that named representation and nominal representation are two different things. My formalisation is in named representation, and it does not involve nominal techniques (such as permutation, support, orbit-finiteness, etc).

Excuse me being imprecise. I was (mis)reading this as a potential first step towards something that could be extended into a fully nominal approach over time.
Although I'm unsure how realistic or useful as an artifact this might be. Seeing your reference to A New Approach to Abstract Syntax with Variable Binding led me to the hope that there was a longtime intention for more nominal heavy techniques.

I'm just trying to order potential directions to read into. I'm mostly searching for some already existing representation where I could compare my theory learnings against and prove some additional lemmas along the way.

I agree it is confusing at first glance that the approach I am using was first defined in a paper using nominal techniques. I would frame it as "a purely named variable approach, inspired by ideas from nominal approaches".

I believe a formalisation of nominal techniques is definitively worth doing, not on top of named representation, but as a standalone formalisation (maybe as another folder under LambdaCalculus?). This is to keep the named representation in a most accessible and beginner-friendly form.

Existing representations elsewhere that I know of include Nominal Isabelle. Possibly less relevant, but you can also check POPLMark and POPLMark Reloaded.

Hi @Haoxuan Yin, I want to thank you again for your patience. Just bad timing and communication on my part as I had not expected to have an internship when we first received your PR. I just finished up leaving a review. Please do let me know if any of my comments are unclear. I do wonder how much the longest of proofs can be compressed and/or extracted into lemmas, but I understand that part of this is named representations being inherently unwieldy.

Hi @Chris Henson , thanks so much for your helpful review. I have addressed your comments and pushed the changes. I have also done a refactoring of all the proofs with more grind, so e.g. Properties.lean has been reduced from 659 lines to 515 lines. Please let me know if you have any further questions or comments!
Hi @Chris Henson , I wanted to check whether you've had a chance to look at the latest changes. Thank you.
No, I've not had a chance yet. The next two weeks I will be in-between jobs and carve out some time to take a look.
Will this eventually be connected with a categorical treatment of nominal sets and the schanuel topos?
I have a port of nominal SSProve. I could split off the nominal part, if noone else has nominal sets in lean yet.

Something like this would be useful

nominal_inductive Tm (𝔸 : Type u)
  | var (a : 𝔸)
  | app (t u : Tm)
  | abs (a : 𝔸) (t : Tm) binds a in t
